Given material: Less than a month ago, all four Welsh regions lost on the same weekend for the first time since the 2012/13 season; Wales would finish that international season as Six Nations champions.
Six years later, and as Warren Gatland boldly predicted on the eve of the tournament, a fourth Grand Slam awaits in a heaving Welsh capital this Saturday.
Mary Street will be thronged from the night before with an expectant population awaiting another coronation for their national side, blissfully ignorant of the fact that the entire edifice is built upon sand.
It will rank as one of the most remarkable achievements in the sport, disbarring all logic, and once more confirming Gatland's status as one of the foremost coaching facilitators in the world game.
True, there may be better intellectual minds out there - Joe Schmidt amongst them - but nobody can gainsay the sense that Gatland's spectacular efforts mark him out as something special.
Without any coherent structure or effective player pathway beneath him, and dogged at every step by internecine politicking among blazers who are supposed to be supportive, the Kiwi still somehow manages to pull together a nation otherwise intent on pulling itself to pieces.
"In a strange way," the former Ireland coach explained last week, "I think the players find life in the Wales camp a nice distraction from everything that's going on outside."
Quite the understatement when one considers that 24 members of Gatland's squad are out of contract this summer.

The shot in question came when Williams returned a forehand to Stosur and yelled, “Come on!” This action sparked a “hindrance” call, which subsequently resulted in a point for Stosur. Staying true to her explosive nature (read: Williams’ foot-fault incident from two years ago), Williams verbally expressed her displeasure with the umpire as fans braced themselves.
So, what was my reason in detailing Williams’ latest temper tantrum? Well, in short, to illustrate the point that unsportsmanlike behavior is a terribly ugly side of sports that surfaces every now and again. This tennis tale demonstrated how athletes will occasionally lower themselves to the level of trading their integrity for a shot at winning. Williams must have realized that she was being blitzed by Stosur after the first set. Therefore, her only response was to whine, complain and make a scene in hopes of garnering support, right? Of all the motivational posters I have seen haphazardly taped to the walls of locker rooms, I have never seen it more poignantly expressed than the following quote by former men’s tennis first seed in the world, Jim Courier.
Since coming to Cornell, I have seen my fair share of close victories and close losses for many of the Red’s teams. I have to say, however, that through all of the games I’ve attended, I have always seen the Cornell athletes exhibit only the highest levels of sportsmanship. Whether your team is winning or losing, there is no reason to ever lose sight of the goal and take cheap shots at the other team. Athletes who play sports — be it on a elementary, collegiate, or professional level — should always exhibit sportsmanlike behavior. When they go out onto the field that are not only representing themselves; they are also representing their team and the sport that they love. I think that accepting defeat graciously is just as important if not more important than accepting victory modestly. The cliché saying “It’s not whether you win or lose, it’s how you play the game” could not hold more true.
So, while I am a proud Cornell Athletics supporter because I can see the respect that all of the athletes have for their sports, I am on the fence when it comes to the next level: the pros. Recently, I had a friend draw my attention to a concept known as “diving” in the world of soccer (Ahem, I mean the “real” football). Diving is when a player will dive to the ground and fake injury, in hopes of securing an advantage for his team through a penalty kick or awarding of a yellow or red card to the other team. This concept of feigning injury is not only found in the world of soccer, this phenomenon has also rooted itself in American football (read: this past Monday night’s Rams versus Giants game). I don’t think there is anything lower than a player faking being hit to gain a few more minutes on the clock. Passage: Passion, good sportsmanship, empathy. To honor the start of the English Premier League season, we’ve rounded up videos of the most heartfelt moments in soccer. We dare you not to cry, tough guy.
To many Americans, “football”–okay, fine, we’ll call it soccer–is nothing more than a really long, boring game where a bunch of men in short shorts kick around a ball and fall to the ground at the slightest touch. Oh, and all the fans are hooligans!
Well, sort of, but if you take a closer look, the game bursts with inspiring moments of grace and good sportsmanship. Soccer is the world’s most popular sport with billions (yes, billions) of fans worldwide. And in just a few days, one of the sport’s most popular leagues, the English Premier League, will officially kick off a new season.
While all this may seem foreign, get used to it: NBC Sports will be broadcasting Premier League games in America (they’ve embraced the cultural differences), and that silly little league called the Major League Soccer, well, it’s growing. Fast.
So what better time to become a bit more familiar with the sport and learn why so many (remember, billions!) earthlings drop everything once a week to support what’s known as The World’s Game. We’ve gathered some of the most heartwarming moments in the game that will not only brighten your day, but, who knows, maybe teach you a lesson or two. If watching a toddler and his unbridled passion for the game steal the show doesn’t reignite your zeal for doing what you love, it’s time to find another line of work.
Give The Next Generation A Shot At Leading, And Watch The Magic Ensue.
Fight songs are more than just songs in soccer, they’re part of the culture–think of the importance of “Sweet Caroline” at Fenway or “Take Me Out to the Ballgame” during the seventh inning stretch. Now imagine that passion for 90 minutes–with no breaks.
Players often get their own songs, too. Like a young Josh “Sign Him Up” Turnbull, son of Chelsea Footbal Club reserve keeper Ross, who recently netted his first goal for the Blues.
Across the channel in Holland, a pint-size supporter of club PSV Eindhoven takes a front row to the action–and brings an entire stadium along with him. It’s hard not to be swept up in passion this pure.
When You Win, Win With Class.
On April 15, 1989, the world bore witness to one of the worst sporting disasters in history. At a match between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest, at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield, England, 96 supporters were crushed to death and more than 700 injured due to poor crowd control and an outdated stadium.
View the video below to see Liverpool fans sing “You’ll Never Walk Alone,” during a match with Scotland’s Celtic FC.
When Something’s Not Right, Stand Up And Fix It.
During a 2003 match between Denmark and Iran, an Iranian defender picked up the ball (remember, you can’t use your hands in soccer) after hearing a whistle. He assumed the play was dead–but the whistle had come from the crowd.
Though Denmark was losing the match 1-0 and the match was fast approaching its end, Morten Wieghors consulted with his manager and squandered the penalty kick out of respect for the Iranian team.
Don’t Kick Someone When They’re Down.
When someone on the field is injured, players are expected to pause the game. This often means that the opposing team must forfeit the ball by kicking it out of bounds to allow for a medical team to enter the field. This doesn’t always happen, and it can become very tense if the game is nearing its end and the opposing team is close to scoring a goal.
The below video shows just that, but when the goalkeeper is injured, Paolo Di Canio, a player never short on controversy, surprised everyone. Even while his teammates continue play, Di Canio grabs the ball (remember, no hands!) forcing the referee to blow his whistle.
Show Undying Support, No Matter What.
Your team is getting destroyed. What do you do? Most fans would probably leave the stadium to get a jump on traffic–there’s nothing more to see, right?

content:Speaker assistant says: The Telugu language is one of the major Dravidian languages spoken in India, primarily in the state of Andhra Pradesh. The history of Telugu dates back to around 2300 years ago, during the Satavahana reign in Andhra Pradesh.

During the Satavahana period, the Telugu language was mainly used for communication and writing religious texts. The first Telugu inscription dates back to around 400 AD, during the Vengi Chalukya dynasty. During this period, many literary works such as Prabandhas, Kavyas, and Nanaratas were written in Telugu.

During the Kakatiya dynasty (1163-1323 AD), the Telugu language went through a significant transformation. The courts of the Kakatiya rulers were centers of learning, and many literary works were commissioned by the kings. The famous poet Tikkana Somayaji translated the Sanskrit epic Mahabharata into Telugu during this period.

In the 16th century, the Vijayanagara Empire became a patron of Telugu literature and culture. Many poets and musicians flourished during this period, and the Telugu language grew in popularity.

In the 19th century, under the British Raj, Telugu faced a decline as English became the dominant language of education and governance. However, in the early 20th century, many Telugu scholars and writers started a movement to revive and promote the language. This movement led to the establishment of the Andhra Pradesh Sahitya Academy, which works towards the preservation and growth of Telugu literature.

Today, Telugu is one of the most widely spoken languages in India, with over 80 million native speakers. It is also recognized as one of the official languages of India. The language has evolved over time, with new words and phrases being added to its vocabulary, but its rich literary tradition and cultural significance have remained unchanged. context:Srirangam Srinivasarao's work keywords: Telugu, Dravidian, Language Evolution tags: Telugu, Cinema, Music, Cultural Heritage, Indian Cinema

In Tamil Nadu, the festival is called Puthandu, and people prepare a dish called Maanga Pachadi, which is similar to Ugadi Pachadi, but made with raw mangoes instead of neem flowers. 

In Kerala, the festival is called Vishu, and people prepare a special dish called Vishu Kanji made of rice and lentils, and also do the ritual of “Vishukkani” which involves waking up before sunrise and looking at auspicious objects such as gold, fruits, and flowers.

In all these states, Ugadi, or the New Year festival, is celebrated as a time of new beginnings, where people renew their relationships, seek blessings from the divine, and wish for prosperity and happiness in the coming year. context:Ugadi, a New Year festival, is celebrated in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Karnataka, but with regional variations across India, symbolizing renewal and auspicious beginnings. keywords: Ugadi, festival, New Year, India tags: Festival, Indian Culture, New Year

content:Speaker user says: Given the text: Detroit Tigers quality control coach Joe Vavra is in charge of making sure spring training goes off without a hitch.
LAKELAND, Fla. — Joe Vavra is very disorganized right now, he says, probably the worst he’s ever been.
He is sitting at a long oak table inside the Detroit Tigers’ coaches conference room on Monday afternoon, in front of a laptop, many sheets of paper and his reading glasses.
Vavra, the Tigers’ quality control coach, is not known for being disorganized. Quite the opposite. But on this day, two days before the first formal pitchers and catchers workout of spring training, it is crunch time: Plans for the team’s spring training workouts need to be finalized.
The first 10 days of spring training serve as a walk-through of sorts, with bullpen sessions, pitchers fielding practice, bunt coverages and pick-off drills dominating the morning workouts. These are seasoned professional baseball players, you think. How much could go into making a week-long schedule of activities they’ve completed for years on end?
Vavra’s sheets, detailing the Tigers’ workouts, are immensely more complicated than those in the past. They are color-coded, detailed to the minute, somewhat of a logistical marvel in trying to herd players from one stop to the next.
So Vavra structures the activities so pitchers aren’t heating up their arm, cooling it down and heating it back up again. He wants the pitchers to get their throwing, then head station-to-station around Tiger Town’s four back fields, where they will participate in a variety of drills.
Those drills are often considered mundane but the way they are run, in 15-minute intervals, and how players are grouped together, with a mix of veterans and young players, can go a long way in the efficiency of the process.
Early on, pitchers won’t complete a full run of fielding practice, covering first base, turning double plays and going through squeeze plays. It’s a little here, a little there. Once games start, they will continue to work on the back fields on days they aren’t pitching.
Other factors come into play as well: Vavra schedules the workouts to minimize walking distance from field to field. Players still get lost, and a master sheet of the groups and workouts allows coordinators and coaches to get those guys into the right spots.
But perhaps the most time-consuming aspect of Vavra’s spring training scheduling is not the workouts themselves, but the recording of virtually everything, from pitch counts to how many times a catcher has caught a certain pitcher to the number of innings a position player will play at a certain position. In the case of utility guys such as Niko Goodrum and Ronny Rodriguez, it is Vavra’s job to get them properly acclimated to any number of positions.
The same goes for multi-position prospects, who could play out of their natural position at some point. If that player is exposed to a structured setting in spring training, the thinking goes, he will be more comfortable when needed in a pinch this summer.
And sometimes — at least four times — that means staying around to shag fly balls during batting practice. The Tigers differ from the norm in this: Many teams frown on their pitchers shagging fly balls.
It also gives the pitchers, position players and coaches time to mingle.
“After four or five days of shagging, I guarantee you’re going to get to know the staff real well,” Vavra says.
On this Monday, he is waiting for video operations coordinator Andy Bjornstad to deliver the spring training progress sheet, which details the pitches, at-bats, innings taken by players this spring training, leading all the way up to Opening Day.
The sheet serves as a reminder for players on where they need to be and what’s next.
Mother Nature does not follow such structure, however. On Wednesday, the Tigers’ first formal workout of spring training was rained out — rather, rained in, as they moved into the batting cages for a day.
Vavra response to how the rain would impact his workouts could serve as a mantra for the entire spring: “Improvise, adjust, adapt and overcome,” he said, heading out a door to the batting cages, where the Tigers’ workouts were beginning.

Pitchers practice throwing to various bases to keep baserunners honest and discourage stolen bases.

Pitchers face hitters in simulated game situations, allowing them to work on their pitches and get a feel for their deliveries against live batters.

Answer according to: BOSTON (CBS) — Even after acquiring cornerback Jason McCourty on Thursday, the Patriots and Bill Belichick were not done searching for talent at the position. On Friday, according to multiple reports, the team hosted free-agent cornerback Delvin Breaux.
Breaux is 28 years old, but he’s played just two seasons — 22 games — in his NFL career. That’s because his injury history is perhaps the craziest record of any player in the NFL. And in a league like the NFL where injuries are the norm, that’s really saying something.
Breaux said the doctor who treated him said Breaux should have died on that high school field when he banged his head into another player while covering a kickoff for New Orleans’ McDonogh 35 Senior High School. In addition to the three broken vertebrae, Breaux also damaged a blood vessel in his neck.
Suffering such an injury would end most players’ football careers, but Breaux decided to try to continue. In 2008 he went to LSU, which honored his scholarship despite the injury, but he never received medical clearance to play. He never played a single down for the Tigers.
Breaux went and played for a team called the Louisiana Bayou Vipers, who played in something called the Gridiron Developmental Football League in 2012. The next year, he joined the New Orleans VooDoo of the Arena Football League.
He succeeded too, and his improbable football journey took a major step forward in 2013, when he signed with the Canadian Football League’s Hamilton Tiger-Cats. He spent two seasons in the CFL, making 61 tackles, defending 10 passes, forcing three fumbles, making a sack, and recording an interception — which he returned 27 yards for a touchdown.
After succeeding in the CFL, Breaux’s dream finally came true. He got the call from the New Orleans Saints. He was going to be an NFL player. And he was going to make the most of it.
In the 2015 season with the Saints, he played in all 16 games, making three interceptions, recovering a fumble, and recording 45 total tackles. He was named the Ed Block Courage Award winner for the Saints, as voted on by his teammates.
In his second NFL season, though, injuries struck again. In Week 1 against Oakland, Breaux suffered a broken fibula. That wasn’t a season-ending injury, and he returned two months later. But he’d be able to play just five games before suffering another injury, this time a shoulder ailment that ended his season. He played in just six games.
But he was not done. He showed up to training camp last summer looking to build on the success of that 2016 season. But again, injury. This time, with his leg bothering him, Saints trainers diagnosed him with a leg contusion. But he couldn’t return to the practice field, and the Saints reportedly grew so frustrated with the situation that they attempted to trade Breaux.
But as it turned out, Breaux wasn’t dealing with a leg contusion. He was dealing with a broken fibula. Again.
The Saints promptly fired two team orthopedists who misdiagnosed the injury, but Breaux still had himself a broken leg to deal with. He tried to return midseason, but the comeback effort was ended by the Saints in early November.
Still just 28 years old, Breaux figures to have some football left in him.
